questions.stem: The area enclosed by the curves \(y=\sqrt{4-x^2}\) and \(y=x^2-2\) is shaded in the diagram below. Which expression could be used to calculate this area?
questions.hint: Find the curves’ intersection points, identify which curve is above the other, and use symmetry about the y-axis.

keyPoints.note: This is the upper semicircle and is the upper curve between the intersections.
Subtract this lower curve from the semicircle.
The enclosed region is symmetric about the y-axis.

steps.explain: At intersection, the y-values are equal.
The right side must be nonnegative; then square both sides.
Expand and solve; reject the root that fails the unsquared equation.
Between the intersections, take upper curve minus lower curve for the vertical strip height.
Use symmetry about the y-axis to double the right-half area.

questions.stem: The area enclosed by the curves \(y=\sin x\) and \(y=\cos x\) is shaded in the diagram. Which expression could be used to calculate this area?
questions.hint: Find where the curves meet (\(\sin x=\cos x\)), then integrate (upper curve \(-\) lower curve).

steps.explain: Find the limits: the curves meet where \(\sin x=\cos x\). Divide by \(\cos x\) (\(\cos x\ne0\)).
These are points \(A\) and \(B\) on the diagram, so the limits are \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) and \(\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\). Options D has the wrong limits.
Between \(A\) and \(B\) the blue curve \(y=\sin x\) is ABOVE the red curve \(y=\cos x\) (e.g. at \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\): \(\sin=1>\cos=0\)).
Write the area with upper \(-\) lower \(=\sin x-\cos x\). Option A is the negative of the area; option C adds the curves.
So the correct choice is option B.

keyPoints.text: Which expression could be used to calculate this area
keyPoints.note: Area between curves: integral of (upper minus lower) between the intersection points.

questions.stem: The graph of \(f(x)=e^{\frac{x}{2}}+1\) is shown. The normal to the graph of \(f\) where it crosses the \(y\)-axis is also shown. Find the equation of the \(\mathbf{normal}\) to the graph of \(f\) where it crosses the \(y\)-axis.
questions.hint: Find the \(y\)-intercept, the gradient of the tangent \(f'(0)\), then the normal gradient \(m_{N}=-\dfrac{1}{m_{T}}\).

steps.explain: Find the point where the graph crosses the \(y\)-axis: put \(x=0\).
Differentiate: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{\frac{x}{2}}=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{\frac{x}{2}}\). Then find the tangent gradient at \(x=0\).
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent: its gradient is the negative reciprocal.
Option C is the TANGENT (gradient \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)); option D has gradient \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\); option B has the wrong sign.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Normal gradient = negative reciprocal of f-prime at the point.

questions.stem: The graph of \(f(x)=e^{\frac{x}{2}}+1\) is shown. The normal to the graph of \(f\) where it crosses the \(y\)-axis is also shown. Find the exact area of the shaded region.
questions.hint: Area \(=\int_{0}^{1}\left(f(x)-\text{normal}\right)dx\), where the normal \(y=2-2x\) meets the \(x\)-axis at \(x=1\).

steps.explain: The normal \(y=2-2x\) cuts the \(x\)-axis where \(y=0\), so \(x=1\): this is the right-hand edge of the shaded region (the vertical line \(x=1\)). The region lies between \(x=0\) and \(x=1\), under the curve and above the normal.
Set up: area \(=\) (upper curve) \(-\) (lower line).
Integrate: \(\int e^{\frac{x}{2}}dx=2e^{\frac{x}{2}}\) (divide by the coefficient \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)).
Substitute the limits.
Alternative check: area under the curve minus the orange triangle (base 1, height 2): \(\left[2e^{\frac{x}{2}}+x\right]_{0}^{1}-\dfrac{1}{2}(1)(2)=(2\sqrt{e}+1-2)-1=2\sqrt{e}-2\). ✓
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Find the exact area of the shaded region
keyPoints.note: Area between curves: integrate upper minus lower between the limits; integrate e to x over 2 as 2e to x over 2.
